summary: ICMP is IP's control and error-reporting protocol. Traceroute turns one ICMP error, Time Exceeded, into a tool for discovering every router on a path by sending probes with increasing TTL.

sections.heading: ICMP basics
sections.body: ICMP messages ride inside IP packets (protocol 1). Each has a Type, a Code, a checksum, and message-specific data. ICMP reports problems; it does not make IP reliable.
bullets: Type 3: Destination Unreachable (code 0 net, 1 host, 2 protocol, 3 port, 4 fragmentation needed and DF set).
Type 11: Time Exceeded (code 0 TTL expired in transit, code 1 reassembly time).

sections.heading: How traceroute works
bullets: Send a probe with TTL = 1. The first router decrements it to 0, drops it, and returns ICMP Time Exceeded, revealing its address.
Send TTL = 2: the second router replies, and so on.
When the probe finally reaches the destination, it answers differently: ICMP Port Unreachable for UDP probes, or Echo Reply for ICMP probes.
Three probes per hop are sent; the round-trip times appear on each line.
sections.code:
$ traceroute example.com
 1  192.168.1.1   1.2 ms  1.0 ms  1.1 ms
 2  10.0.0.1      8.4 ms  8.1 ms  8.6 ms
 3  * * *                       <- no reply (filtered)
 4  93.184.216.34 20.3 ms ...

sections.heading: Probe types
bullets: Linux/Unix traceroute: UDP to high ports (33434 upward) by default; ICMP and TCP modes available.
TCP traceroute (e.g. to port 443) passes firewalls that block UDP/ICMP.

sections.heading: Reading the output
bullets: An asterisk means no reply within the timeout: the router may rate-limit or block ICMP, not necessarily drop traffic.
A sudden latency jump that continues to later hops signals a slow link; a spike on one hop only is often just ICMP deprioritization.
Different probes can take different paths because of load balancing.

sections.body: `ping` sends Echo Requests with identifier and sequence numbers so replies can be matched; it reports round-trip time and loss. Use `ping -M do -s 1472` to test the path MTU with DF set.

subtopics.title: Path MTU discovery depends on ICMP

sections.body: ICMP type 3 code 4 tells senders to shrink packets. Filtering all ICMP causes PMTU black holes where TCP connections hang once large packets are sent.

bullets: Load-balanced paths show an inconsistent route.
Return paths may differ (asymmetric routing), so per-hop RTT is misleading.
Firewalls may block probes or replies.

sections.body: MTR runs continuous traceroute with per-hop loss and latency statistics. Paris-traceroute keeps flow identifiers constant so probes follow one load-balanced path.
ICMPv6 (RFC 4443) also carries Neighbor Discovery and Packet Too Big, so it must not be blocked as casually as ICMPv4.

takeaways: ICMP reports errors and diagnostics; Type 11 Time Exceeded enables traceroute.
Traceroute increases TTL by one each probe and records who replies.
The destination replies with Port Unreachable (UDP) or Echo Reply (ICMP).
Asterisks and latency spikes need careful interpretation.
